utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Monday, and good afternoon to the accused. Mr. Pusic is back with us. A special good afternoon to you. Good afternoon to the Defence counsel and to Mr. Stringer and his team. Not to forget the interpreters, the usher, and -- ushers, and registrars. We're going to continue with our work, but I'll first give the floor to the registrar who has some IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Zelenika Mirko. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00864. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00865. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00866. The list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit number IC 00867. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I have three oral rulings. Mr. Registrar, can we first briefly move into private session for the first decision.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second oral ruling. On the 15th of October, 2008, the Prosecution filed a motion asking the Trial Chamber to cancel the testimony of Witness Neven Tomic scheduled to start on the 27th of October or, in the alternative, to postpone his testimony until the Prlic Defence has disclosed a more expansive 65 ter summary together with documents related to interviews that took place between Neven Tomic and Milan Cvikl. As to the first issue, the Trial Chamber recalls its 13th of October, 2008, oral ruling in which it ruled that the Prlic Defence had disclosed enough supplemental information for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution to be able -- and for the Prosecution to prepare its cross-examination. The motion by the Prosecution is therefore moot on this issue. With regard or on account of time constraints connected with the forthcoming testimony of Neven Tomic, the Trial Chamber asked the Prlic Defence to file its response on the second part of the Prosecution motion related to the alleged interview of Neven Tomic with Milan Cvikl by the 22nd of October, 2008. Third oral ruling. It is an important one, and I'm going to read it out slowly. Oral ruling related to the testimony of the expert witness Milan Cvikl. On the 16th of October, 2008, the Prosecution filed a new motion for the dismissal or postponement of the testimony of expert witness Milan Cvikl on the ground, inter alia, of late disclosure by the Prlic Defence of the expert's report. The testimony of expert witness Milan Cvikl is scheduled, based on the schedule filed by the Prlic Defence, to testify as of the 17th of November, 2008. After careful review, the Trial Chamber has ruled that the testimony of witness Milan Cvikl shall be postponed until further notice and shall issue a written decision as soon as possible. So, Mr. Karnavas, in other words, Milan Cvikl will not come on the 17th of November, 2008, and he's likely to appear in 2009, a date we have not specified yet. Furthermore, the issue might come up in a similar way for another witness due to testify after Cvikl because we are in the same situation, since the Trial Chamber to date still not has the expert report. So it can be expected that will the second expert witness will be heard in 2009 at a date that will be agreed, I suppose, with the Stojic Defence or with the Praljak Defence depending on everybody's availability. Have you understood, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. A report was filed last night at approximately -- I believe it was 9.30, maybe 10.00 at night. This should be -- perhaps it hasn't been circulated yet. I'm told that it is -- it has been circulated. It actually -- it's two reports. In total, it's about, I believe, 40 pages, but if the decision is to postpone it, we certainly would appreciate having notice so then we could advise our expert. The same thing with the first expert. We would want to know as much as, you know, time in advance because the gentleman is a Member of Parliament in Slovenia, and so he could juggle around his schedule. And getting back, if I may, Your Honour, to the second decision, I can categorically state as I've stated in the past, but I'll do so again, and if you wish I can do it in writing: There are no interview statements between Mr. Tomic and Mr. Cvikl. Now, what I have done, what I have done, because I anticipated this sort of decision, I wrote to Mr. Cvikl and asked him to kindly put down the methodology of these particular interviews and -- so that there would be some clarity. That way, we could provide that information to you and to the Prosecution. I have not heard back from him, perhaps because of his schedule, but when I do get that information, I will pass it on. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, with regard to the second expert report, the Prlic Defence is telling us that it is about 40 pages long. So you'll have to take a stance very quickly. If you don't have any problem with it, just say so, and the expert witness can then come very soon. But should there be a problem -- and now I'm turning to the other Defence counsel. Is there a problem with translating it -- translating the 40 pages into B/C/S, then the other Defence counsel have to advise us, but apparently there's no problem. Yes, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The second report was actually done in Serbian, and the Prlic Defence at its own expense translated it into English to expedite it, knowing that it would take forever because of the backlog. So we did it, and so we have it. We circulated the English. The B/C/S version hasn't been circulated yet, but we will do so probably today, later today, but my staff was working very late yesterday to collate it and circulate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. There's one matter arising out of the oral ruling which I'm asked to raise, and -- well, there's two matters, in fact, that arise out of the postponement of the testimony of my learned friend Mr. Karnavas's expert, Mr. Cvikl, and it's this: We hope that this decision will not impact upon when we are expected to start our Defence case; in other words, that in the event that Mr. Karnavas's case is shortened, we won't be expected to start earlier than we have anticipated because I'm told that scheduling has already taken place to some degree, at least, and so that would prejudice us. The second matter, Your Honours, that I'm asked to raise is that we have a very strong preference, and in fact it's our application that this expert Cvikl gives evidence before we start our Defence case because as I understand it, his testimony is relevant to testimony that we will call in our Defence case, in particular, one of the Defence experts, and we want to hear what Mr. Cvikl is going to say before we call that expert to give evidence. Your Honours, those are the matters that I have been asked to raise for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, since you're on your feet, you'll be able to answer straightaway. In the schedule you prepared, when did you plan your first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the beginning of December, 1st of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your first witnesses could come early December. No problem. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that that's exactly the case. There wouldn't be a problem with witnesses coming at the beginning of December, but with the caveat that I've been asked to raise that we would very much like to dispense and complete the testimony of Mr. Cvikl before we start our Defence case. In other words, we -- to that extent, we were opposed to the Prosecution application or suggestion to interpose Mr. Cvikl in the Defence case of Mr. Stojic. We'd like to finish with that case before we start ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Judge Trechsel has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Two questions, actually, Mr. Khan. The first is, is it your point that you would not even wish to start before you have heard the expert Cvikl? And the second, if not, if you could live with having him sometimes during your own defence, when do you plan that to end? I could probably figure it out by looking back in the paper, but you will be able to tell me right away, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you'll give me a moment, I think my learned leader wishes to add something to me. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, dealing with the second question first, we don't know. We don't have an approximation at the moment off the top of my head, at least, as to when we hope to finish our Defence case. I'm sure that could be given in a very ballpark fashion a little bit later, but the first witness was going to be an expert, and it was -- the first witness for the Stojic Defence was going to be an expert, and it was for that reason that I was instructed to request that we finish with Mr. Cvikl before we start our case. Your Honour, the other matter which, of course, may impact upon your determination of this matter is that, of course, there are some pending 92 bis, 92 ter witnesses that my learned friend has to put before the Trial Chamber. So that may enable all parties to be happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, yes, we sought some information from the translation department to know how long it would take for the report to be translated into B/C/S for the sake of the accused, and we were told that they needed two months. Today is the 20th of October, so 20th of November, and then 20th of December. In other words, the report cannot be made available to the accused in the best possible case before the 20th or the 21st of December. So at first blush, it's not possible for your first witness to come prior to the 22nd of December. However, you are absolutely right. Mr. Karnavas is still due to give us a list of 92 bis witnesses. Indeed, should the Prosecutor would wish to cross-examine some of them, we could have them before you start, and your expert could come in January. We could start in January, both Mr. Cvikl straight after the recess, and then you would start after him. But we still need the 92 bis list. Mr. Karnavas promised to do it very quickly last week, but it has not been done yet. When can we expect it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one additional matter with your permission. I'm most grateful for that clarification. I was told just whilst I was on my feet that it's important we view the matter, that we hear Mr. Cvikl before we start our Defence case, that the issue regarding the translation, I'm told that arrangements will be made from -- by the Stojic Defence to independently get that translated so not as to overburden the court translation department, CLSS. So, Your Honours, I've just been told that at the moment, but that may expedite matters. I don't envisage that -- well, maybe I've got the wrong end of the stick. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, no. I think -- that offer, it was quickly retracted. I think -- as the January date was mentioned that we will not undertake that leviathan task. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, regarding your 92 bis witnesses, when can we expect the list? Now you understand the urgency of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do. I do, Mr. President. If we could just go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Mr. President and Your Honours and counsel. I just have a number of responses to the various items that have been raised. In respect of the translation into the Serbo-Croatian of Mr. Cvikl's report, what I'm hearing or what I understand is that really isn't going to happen until after the 1st of the year or that it's going to push Mr. Cvikl into 2009. And if that is the case, I just wanted to make sure I understand that correctly because based upon not only the translation issue but the size and the complexity of the report and the volume of documentation that's involved, we're going to need at least until that time-frame to prepare ourselves. That was my first point. We were interested to hear that the Stojic Defence is intending to lead off their case in chief with an expert. We've not yet discussed our -- the fact that the Trial Chamber's earlier Scheduling Order required the Defence reports to be disclosed to the Prosecution on the 31st of March, 2008. Now, I'm concerned already that we're already being forced into the same position now that we've had with the other experts. I don't know who the expert is. I have not seen this person's report. This person is apparently intended to testify beginning the first week of December, and again, that's unacceptable. The date for disclosure of the expert report has not been met. We have 30 days to file our response to the report under Rule 94 bis, and so here we are being set up right off the bat into a situation which I think is prejudicial to the Prosecution in its ability to prepare to meet this evidence. In respect of the Rule 92 bis witnesses that the Prlic team is still intending to call, obviously we haven't seen the statements of four of those witnesses, and the Prosecution would obviously reserve its position on that. I think that it's likely the Prosecution is going to at least request that one or more of the eight witnesses be called, and I'm not saying necessarily it will be all eight, but from what we know about the witnesses and what we know about the four witnesses who have testified previously and were - I agree - subject to cross-examination previously, I think at the moment Prosecution's inclined toward requesting that at least one of them come for cross-examination. We've not arrived at a final position on that, but once we have counsel's final submissions on all of his 92 bis witnesses, we'll file a prompt response to that so that the Trial Chamber can arrange or factor in whatever scheduling may be necessary. And then one final remark, and this relates now to the Trial Chamber's decision to postpone the testimony of Mr. Cvikl. Again, because he was schedule to come rather soon, we prepared over the weekend a response to the submission of the Prlic Defence that was filed last Friday. That was a Prlic submission asking that about 89 documents be added to their Rule 65 ter list, and all of these documents are linked to the expert report of Mr. Cvikl. Now, we filed a fast response, again, because of the scheduling, and we thought it would advance the discussion to get that filed quickly. However, as the Trial Chamber will find, that response was largely driven by the possibility that Mr. Cvikl might be coming to testify beginning on the 17th of November. Now, I just thought it would be useful to inform the Trial Chamber and the parties that in -- in light of the Trial Chamber's ruling today and in light of the fact that Mr. Cvikl won't be testifying until next year, our position in respect of adding those documents to the Rule 65 ter list is likely to change. Certainly, I think the Prosecution's in a position now to show greater flexibility in terms of adding those to the list now that we will, it appears, have sufficient time to assimilate those. However, I'm informed that about 58 of those documents we don't have translations for yet. So ultimately our response will depend upon the timing of our receiving the translations. But rather than everyone going away and reading the response that we just filed earlier today, I can inform all of you that our position on this is going to now be changed I think in view of the postponement of Mr. Cvikl's testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, one little problem. You told us that you were planning to call an expert. We don't have the expert's report. The Trial Chamber is about to issue a written decision, and it will request to have expert reports two months before they appear because you've got the 30 days under Rule 94 bis, and everybody's got to prepare for the testimony, of course. Today is the 20th of October. Now, if your expert were to come to the 1st of December, the 2-month period is not complied with. So when are we going to receive your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm most grateful, Mr. President. The expert, first and foremost, is Mr. Davor Marijan. He's listed on our 65 ter list, and I received an English copy of that report last week in English. It will be served upon the Prosecution by the end of this week. So I've been -- we've been quite timely, I think, between receipt of the report in English that I can read and service upon the Prosecution, which will be by the end of this week. It's a short report. It's 60 pages at the moment. It's not a long report at all, and given the time line that has been detailed previously, of course, the Prosecution will get, in all likelihood, and it's October still, the two months or thereabouts to prepare. But this is a quite a discrete report of about 60 pages at the moment. They will get it at the end of this week, and they are, of course, not being set up right off the bat, and it's a bit premature in my respectful submission to contend at this juncture that there's any prejudice at all. They will get it at the end of this week, and I think when it is seen, when it's read by my learned friend, they will have more than sufficient time to deal with that report. Your Honours, I hope that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. As far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, we shall see how things stand much more clearly when we have the eight 92 bis reports of Mr. Prlic, and we want the Prosecution to tell us who they want to cross-examine. I won't quote any names. There are some people on the first list who have high-ranking jobs, and I'm sure they have a very tight schedule, and these people might not be able to come at short notice given their agenda. So we would like the Prosecution to let us know if and when they wish to cross-examine these witnesses. Then the Prlic team will say when they can come. Mr. Stringer, do we agree on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I would only add that once we have the Prlic Defence motion - and I'm assuming there's going to be a motion relating to all eight of the 92 bis witnesses that are being proposed - once the motion is filed, I can assure the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution will respond very quickly. We know now all of them, who they are, and we know -- obviously, we have the testimony of four of them. So once we have the motion for all eight, we'll be able to respond very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, it's somewhat difficult given that there is this pending 92 bis motion dealing with these eight witnesses, but I wonder if it's possible at all at this juncture to get an indication from the Trial Chamber as to when we on behalf of Bruno Stojic should be ready to start our Defence case, when in January. I don't know if Your Honours can give any guidance at this juncture, but it would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, listen. If CLSS takes two months, this means that nothing can be done before the 20th of December; and if you can only start examining the witnesses after this witness, Milan Cvikl would come at the beginning of January, and your first witness would come straight after him. I don't see how we can do it any other way. But if you have another suggestion, please share it with us. We are very happy to hear of any intelligent suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's been a circular from the President of the Tribunal that the court recess - and I stand to be corrected - is until the 9th of January. Is the Trial Chamber also minded to have the court recess for the same period, or would there be any variance from what the Tribunal is going to be enjoying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, you are now addressing another issue which we have already addressed. To begin with, we had thought of starting before the 9th of January, but one of the Judges sitting on this Bench will not be available. And as far as I'm concerned, I will not be available from the 12th to the 19th. Therefore, the winter recess might last even longer, i.e., four weeks, which means that our last hearing should be held on the 12th of December, and we would resume on the 9th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just one remark, Mr. President. I don't want by my silence for the Trial Chamber to conclude that the Prosecution necessarily accepts, with respect, the submissions of the Stojic team. If they want to know what Mr. Cvikl is going to say, they can read the very lengthy detailed report that he's submitted. It's not clear to me that they will be in the dark about what his testimony will be if they read his report. It doesn't seem to follow that they need to wait to see what he comes and says when in fact it's likely the Trial Chamber will be considering the report in advance of his testimony, possibly admitting parts of it into evidence even before he testifies. If the time-frame stands as it is with the witness coming for four days of testimony, I think -- I would hope that it's fair to assume that most of that time will be spent on cross-examination, assuming that the expert report or parts of it come into evidence. So everybody knows or will know what Mr. Cvikl is going to say, assuming he says and adopts what's in his report. So it doesn't seem clear to me why we have to stop everything on the Stojic side until after he's testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, just one small point of detail. On looking at your schedule, I noticed that you had planned to hear Mr. Cvikl as of the 17th of November for four days. Had you planned to have these four days for cross-examination, or had you included examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, initially we had Mr. Cvikl down for six hours. We then reduced him to four hours, that is, for the direct examination. We anticipated the rest of the week would be taken up both by direct and other cross from both aisles. It is conceivable that the direct may be shorter. I don't know. I mean, I can assure the Trial Chamber that the report, which is rather comprehensive, and anyone who looked at it can see that there are actually two aspects of it and perhaps three. The first part is sort of general, dealing with the former Yugoslavia and the general system. That's to give everyone some context. And then it goes into an analysis of the various legal instruments that were passed by the Croatian Community and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna as well as a comparative analysis of what was happening elsewhere. I don't think, and I would agree with the Prosecution here, that there aren't going to be any surprises. What -- there maybe some amplification as to certain areas in order to give it more context, and of course, we're hoping that there would be questions from the Bench and from the others that would flush out any issues that remain unclear, but the report is rather comprehensive. And again, we haven't sat down to go through the report with the gentleman, and we don't know to what extent the Prosecution's going to be objecting to the entire report, parts of it, or what have you. But we put down four hours for cross -- for direct examination, and we thought that that was rather modest considering the overall scope of his testimony even with the report because parts of the report may not necessarily be -- I don't mean to offend anyone, but may not necessarily be accessible to everyone because they may not be familiar with economics, you know, and maybe the writing style is somewhat rigid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, one last question. We understood that you established a connection between your witness Davor and Cvikl, and you wanted your conditions Davor to come and testify after Mr. Cvikl. That, I understand perfectly well. That is not why I am raising this issue. I'd like to know, on the list of your other witnesses, could you not call to testify other witnesses and separate Davor from Cvikl? Couldn't you call other witnesses that would address other topics other than that one? To avoid wasting time, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. If I may, I would like to reply to this. We have built our entire defence strategy on this basis: First of all, the witness named in our 65 ter list will tell us about the structure of the defence department, and then he will pave the way for other witnesses who will come along and build on his explanation, the explanation provided in his expert finding. This is how we organised our defence. First of all, it depends or relies on the expert report. We fully respect the fact as it is that we should not be causing any undue delays; but as things are now, there will be no undue delays. If we take into account witnesses that might be 92 bis witnesses for the OTP pursuant to a proposal of the Prlic Defence and then the 92 ter witness statements that will be tendered, it seems to follow that there is no way we can start before the 12th of December, which is when the recess begins. Therefore, I do not believe that we shall in any way affect this or cause any undue delays in relation to any witnesses during the Prlic or Stojic Defence cases. Just for the benefit of the record, I wish to make it known to everyone that the Stojic Defence does not believe that there could be any traps for the Stojic Defence in Mr. Cvikl's evidence. However, our very first witness is also an expert, and he will tell us about all the different segments of the defence department, including those addressed by Mr. Cvikl. Therefore, we believe it would be a good thing for us to first hear Mr. Cvikl, which would then allow us to pose certain questions to our own expert. In the best of cases, we could use this to refute Mr. Cvikl's evidence. We do not believe that this is a trap that is being laid for us, but we do think that this would, nevertheless, be a good thing. And we could perhaps use this to readjust our case later on, but that could only happen if our witness comes before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your witness Davor is, in strategic terms, important because he will be the cornerstone of your defence strategy, and all the other witnesses will come after him. That, I have understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to have confirmed by Mr. Karnavas that his second expert must be number two and must come after Cvikl because if that were not the case, then I regard it as not excluded that he can be heard still before the recess, and it would be for Mr. Stringer or for the Prosecutor to tell us as soon as possibly what their view is on this, Mr. Karnavas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with that witness, and it's a she.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with that witness coming before Mr. Cvikl. That's not a problem. I mean, we would need -- for scheduling we'd want to inform her, but we had hoped that if there was a delay and if the Prosecution were not going to object to it and if she could make it in her schedule to call her even a week earlier, so -- but we remain rather flexible on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If you can give an answer, but I don't want to pressure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. The report was just received by us today. We're reviewing it at the moment. It's troubling to us that no one except the Prosecution seems to be bothered at all by the fact that these experts' reports are being filed so many months after the deadline set by the Trial Chamber. And maybe the Trial Chamber's granted extensions of time that the Prosecution doesn't know about. I don't know, but we wouldn't be in this situation at least if there hadn't been some advance notice and possibly a submission to say, "Look, we need more time," but none of that's happened, and here we are at the very end of the Prlic case, and we're being put in the position of having to respond when in fact we shouldn't even be having this conversation. But be that as it may, all I can say at this juncture, Your Honour, is that we're reviewing the report. I'll go back, and we're going to confer, and I can assure the Trial Chamber that we will inform you very soon, within a matter of days, whether we feel like we can go ahead. I can assure the Trial Chamber and counsel that I cannot picture us agreeing to move forward the date of the witness's testimony by one week. I think the question is whether we agree to go ahead as scheduled for that final week of November or whether in fact it's our position that -- whether we persist in our position that the expert report as well as that of Mr. Cvikl be excluded for having failed to meet the time deadline; or secondly, whether it should be postponed at some point later than the last week of November, but we will inform you of our position on that within a matter of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could just briefly respond. The Prosecution was giving us their expert reports in the middle of their case. Perhaps the gentleman wasn't here at the time. Mr. Sudetic, for instance, they promised him as an expert. He wasn't in the end called because he was rejected as such being that he was an employee of the OTP and not an expert of any source. But nonetheless, for months they kept saying that they were going to call him. For months, we were waiting for a report; and when we got it, it was binders and binders and binders, yet I heard no apology from the Prosecution. Expert Miller was similarly in that fashion. In fact, with him, they put him on, and then it was afterwards they added documents to the 65 ter list. We, on the other hand, have taken the other route. So we are prepared to answer those questions in motion. We looked at the rules; we looked at the rulings; we looked at the deadlines; and it was quite interesting that the Prosecution up until a month ago had absolutely no problem. And all after sudden, as the case is getting closer and closer to the end of the Prlic case, now it seems that every Monday we spent arguing about procedural issues, and I wonder why. So I take offence to this somehow we have missed these deadlines. We have been consistent. They've known about it; they haven't complained; and now they're trying to turn this into an advantage, and that's pure poppycock.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: One brief response, Mr. President. Every Prosecution report of every expert was provided many, many months in advance to the Defence teams before anyone was in the position of having to cross-examine -- or consider or prepare cross-examination of a Defence witness or to prepare a Rule 94 bis response to a Prosecution expert report. We know the difficulties in assembling this sort of evidence with these sorts of expert witnesses, and if any of the Defence teams had ever approached the Prosecution to say, "Look, we need more time. We're going to get these filed, but we're not going to be able to do it within the deadlines set by the Trial Chamber," there would have been no objection whatsoever from us on that. The problem and the reason why the objections are coming in at this late stage is because a 200-page expert report of an economist, a former member of the World Bank, and current Member of Parliament of the State of Slovenia, his expert report was disclosed to us on the 10th of October accompanied by about 5.000 pages of documents, and it was proposed that we would file our 94 bis response to that report and then be prepared to cross-examine this witness during the week of November 17th; and the Prosecution, Mr. President, never put any of the Defence teams in that situation. We would have had no problem to extensions of deadlines for filing the report so long as it didn't prejudice us in time. Now, I recognise the Trial Chamber is postponing the testimony. That's fine. But I can tell you, it's caused a week or so of very nervous preparation on the Prosecution side because it's all come in so late in the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not, with your leave, going to address the substance of my learned friend's observations on this issue. In my respectful submission, while it's not agreeing with much of what my learned friend says, the issue is moot, that the Trial Chamber has indicated that it is in the throes of issuing an order that expert reports must be given to the other parties two months before the witness is called. In those circumstances, Your Honour, I think there can be no contention of prejudice or being disadvantaged, and it will not help clarify matters, to rebut what my learned friend has said. So I have no other observations than the issue is moot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we will close the debate on this issue. I think everybody knows what it is all about. The Trial Chamber will hand out a written decision on this matter very soon. As you have understood, we are jeopardised by the translation deadlines, which take two months. There's nothing we can do about that. We shall now bring the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Usher, could you go and fetch him, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Can you give us your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Marinko Simunovic, born on the 28th of June, 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a degree in engineering. I'm deputy director of the general directorate for civilian airlines in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you already testified before a court of law on those events which unfolded in the former Yugoslavia, or are you testifying for the first time today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to convey to you some information which will shed some light on the way in which these proceedings will unfold. You will be asked to answer questions which will be put to you by the Defence teams, and you have already seen these documents with Mr. Karnavas when you prepared for this hearing. After that, Defence counsel representing the other accused - they are sitting on your left - will put questions to you as well. The Prosecutor who is on your right, there are two of them on the team today. Well, they will put questions to you. This will be part of our cross-examination. I think it will be Mr. Stringer who will put questions to you. The four Judges that make up the Bench and that are sitting in front of you will put questions to you in the course of these examinations. Please try and be as accurate as you can when you answer. If you don't understand the meaning of a question, please don't hesitate, and ask the person who has put the question to you to rephrase it even if it is a judge putting a question which seems unclear to you. Don't hesitate, and ask to have the question repeated to you. We have breaks every hour and a half. We shall have a break in half an hour's time because we have spent 45 minutes on procedural issues. You have taken the solemn declaration, which means that you are now a witness of the court, and you may not contact Mr. Karnavas. If you do not feel well at any time, raise your hand if you wish the hearing to be suspended for short time. Don't hesitate. If you wish to put a question yourself, you may do so. Mr. Karnavas, you now have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to start by asking you some questions on your background, and then we're going to go right into the events that are relevant for us. You've told us that you are an engineer by training. As I understand it, you got your engineering degree from -- was that in Sarajevo or Zagreb? No, I'm sorry. It was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Mostar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And prior to the war, as I understand it, you worked in the aviation industry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I was working for the Sokol Mostar company in the new programme development section. If you need any detail, I'll be happy to provide those as well. Ten years of experience with the Sokol enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you to speak slowly because everything is being translated, and so if there could be a pause, as well, that would be most useful and helpful. What exactly did you do for Sokol, just so we -- if you could just tell us very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. I worked on projects, mostly ground equipment for former military programmes for the special purpose Sokol industry production.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I later worked on projects that had to do with civil aviation. In 1988 and throughout 1989, I was with the joint team in the airbus headquarters in Toulouse, France. I was helping design the 330 and 340 airbus models, the parts for which were at the time built by the Mostar Sokol company, of which I was a part. The last project that I worked on was producing documents, technical documents and the technical documentation for a seaborne minibus, which is another thing that the Sokol company was supposed to build at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And now, where were you -- or where did the war find you? Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The war caught me in my family home. I was still living with my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In Mostar. Radoca [phoen] was the name of the neighbourhood. It's in the south of Mostar, very close to the Sokol factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we've heard lots of testimony about the events that occurred in and around Mostar in 1992, April and May. If you could tell us, up until what point did Sokol operate during that period?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Sokol officially continued to operate up until mid-April. It was getting very difficult, however, and the number of people for security-related reasons had stopped showing up for work. All of the production activity had already ground to a halt by the second half of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: It proved impossible for a number of people to simply report for work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we're speaking of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When did you stop working at Sokol?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I stopped working -- well, I don't remember the exact date, but it was sometime early in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we know, and we're going to hear lots of testimony from you, that you were involved in the Red Cross in the Mostar municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When did you begin working for the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I started working for the Mostar Red Cross on the 28th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly wait before he starts answering the question because he understands English, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You're going to have the wait. Listen, you know, because there's -- we need to have a little pause. All right. And -- well, it seems that there was some sort of a gap between the time that you stopped working at Sokol and the time you started working with the Red Cross. Could you please tell us, where were you; what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. I spent some of that time in an area that was at the time surrounded by the JNA and the reservists. I was no longer able to go to work. Later on, when the explosion occurred on the 3rd of April, the explosion in Mostar, most of the population from Radoc [phoen] moved to the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I would occasionally go back to Radoc on two occasions, to be more specific, to get some things that I'd left behind and that my family now needed because they'd fled Mostar as soon as the 3rd. They first went to Ljubuski and then later on to the peninsula of Peljesac: My father, my mother, my two children, and my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, how is it you got involved in the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this has to do with the previous story. They had gone on before me, but they didn't bring any of their stuff. So I went back to Rodoc in order to get some things that I could then take through and bring them back to my family. There was this one time that I was on my way to visit my family in Peljesac. I drove back through Baska Voda, which is where my grandparents were. I wanted to see them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: And that's where I was struck by a health problem, a back problem. I was bedridden for a full ten days. Once I was able to move again, I had already learned that there was some refugees from Mostar and other areas in Baska Voda, and there was a humanitarian organisation that was operating there, and the name of this humanitarian organisation was Croatian's Young For Herceg-Bosna's Young. I started working with that organisation, and I tried to do whatever I could to organise aid for Mostar because I knew what the situation was like in the town. Towards the end of that month, on or about the 26th, I managed to have the first aid shipment to Mostar --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which month are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- and I started getting in touch with the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which month --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The 11th of May. That's when it began, and then I stayed in Baska Voda until the 28th of June, and I had also visited my family in Peljesac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was the date or month when you made -- when you took the shipment to Mostar? What month was that? May, June, July, August?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, how is it that you got this job at the Red Cross? I mean, you went from being an engineering in the avionics industry to distributing humanitarian aid. How did you get that? How did you make that transition?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The transition occurred on account of a mere accident. I simply met those people while I was over there who were involved with that humanitarian organisation. Then I also knew some people who were dealing with logistics in the town itself, and that was when I brought the aid there. They recognised my ability to work with speed and efficiency and that I could get aid relatively quickly. I had already got in touch with a number of people, and I also had a lot of experience when I worked with the Sokol team, some projects. I knew how to get those things up and running, and some people were aware of my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, who appointed you to this position?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what position did you start at?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was first appointed coordinator for the work of the Red Cross in war, and then there was the proper procedure for me to be appointed executive manager of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how long did you work for the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I worked with the Mostar Red Cross from the 28th of June, 1992, to the 1st of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I left, and I became the chief secretary of the BH Federation Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when did you finally finish working with the Red Cross in BiH?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I left the Red Cross altogether on the 3rd of October, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to focus your attention to the period when you first started working with the Red Cross. If you could please tell us how the Red Cross in Mostar municipality was organised, number one; and number two, what sort of activities did it carry out, if any?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: When I joined the Red Cross, the Red Cross worked under a statute that dated to a period before the war, but it, the Red Cross or I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can't tell what the subject is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- actively joined the developments that had to do with war in Mostar at the time. However, people who were in charge of the Red Cross were not getting any younger and were lacking the energy or the stamina to lead the Red Cross in this newly arisen situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I need you to listen to my questions and only answer my questions. Right now, we need to figure out, what did the Red Cross do as an organisation? If I want to know about who was leading it, I'll ask you. So what was the Red Cross doing as an organisation because it may change from country to country, region to region.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Red Cross distributed humanitarian aid. It also administered first aid in a purely medical sense. It collected charity and blood donations. It also mediated in the search for missing persons on behalf of the international committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you joined, what was the size of the staff?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: If you mean the operative structures of the Red Cross, seven or eight people. The warehouse and all the other activities, over 20 persons, some volunteers and some employees of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about physical facilities? What sort of facilities did it have other than an office?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We had a reserve warehouse in the building. We had a couple of computers, the ones that were in use at the time. We had a certain rolling stock, one small vehicle and one freight vehicle, and we also had some equipment that was used for rendering assistance or first aid to the people who were needing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, that leads me to my next question. The aid itself, where was that coming from that you were distributing?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the aid was coming from various donors. The main collaborator of the Red Cross was the ICRC, by definition, as well as the UNHCR and other organisations that expressed interest to provide help to Mostar at the time. There were also lots of donations arriving in the town through people who were engaged outside of the country, and all this aid was addressed to the Red Cross in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you mentioned the ICRC and the UNHCR. What were the other organisations that were in and around Mostar at the time providing aid?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the Red Cross, our partners were Merhamet and Caritas, and later the Red Crescent and other locally based organisations established in the area of Mostar municipality, and they had their own sources of aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before I ask you to describe to us how the aid was distributed, if you could explain to us whether the Mostar municipal Red Cross was tied into any other regional or state organisations, you know, Red Cross organisations.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Mostar Red Cross initially did not have any contacts with the Red Cross of Bosnia-Herzegovina, since all the communication lines had been severed with these institutions. At the time when I joined them, there were -- there was already a regional Red Cross established of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and I got involved in the operation of the coordinating body that was monitoring the activities of other Red Cross organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this regional organisation, to what extent was it influencing the activities in Mostar, that is, the Mostar municipal Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Only in that part where we were obliged, according to the statute and other documents on which we operated, we were obliged to maintain the mandate of the International Red Cross. Otherwise, there was no intention on their part to influence our work in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can you please tell us whether you know about other municipalities, if they had a similar Red Cross organisation, and if so, how it operated.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, every municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina had a Red Cross organisation established, and all these organisations of the Red Cross, in compliance with their capabilities and needs, attempted and made effort to provide assistance to people who were in hardships due to everything that was happening in our country at the time, either to a greater or to a lesser extent depending on their capacity, the situation on the ground, the number of the staff available, et cetera. However, Mostar was in a specific situation. The town of Mostar was the place where -- which had so many people in need, and at what -- at one point more than 90 per cent of the population was in need of assistance or aid of all sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're going to get to that in more detail, but first, can you tell us to what extent the Mostar municipal Red Cross had any relations with the local government, the Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Only to the extent that with a view to the response to the situation we had common ground. The social welfare institutions had a compatible mandate to the one that we had, and in that specific area we had more close ties and frequent meetings. As far as the influence of the executive authorities is concerned, we had a complete free hand to operate as we wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what about the executive authority, the HVO HZ HB? Was there any relationship or any association between that executive body and the Mostar municipal Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Only in the event that there was a need for that for whatever reason that we had to ask permission to import some staff, and we needed papers issued by these institutions. So these were the only situations that we needed to contact with them. Otherwise, that was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated -- you told us that there were several organisations providing aid. Were these organisations, along with the Red Cross, coordinating in any way their efforts, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These organisations, also by the intention of the government, worked in concert; and they established a coordinating body that monitored the situation on the ground, collected information about the people in need, the situation about the inflow of humanitarian aid, and the direct distribution of that humanitarian aid on the ground. That was a very productive and constructive work that this body did. Meetings took place on a weekly basis. We always had unlimited access to the information about which organisation received what kind of aid so that we can prepare a joint plan of distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps before the break you can tell us in very -- sort of general terms how aid was distributed once it was received by the Red Cross so we sort of have a general picture because then after the break we'll go into the documents.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In view of its potential and available capacities, the Red Cross was entrusted with coordinating and running the database of the inflow of aid. The aid was distributed in the following way: All the humanitarian organisations that were participating in this coordinating body would provide their respective information about how many tons or units of certain goods they had on stock in their warehouses. This kind of information would be fed to a joint database, and then with regard to the number of users in local communities where the distribution points were located, we issued orders to our commissioners, local commissioners, to take over the stuff, and they would come with trucks to load it. For example, two tons of flour were loaded from one storehouse from Merhamet and other stuff from Caritas, just 2 or 300 litres of cooking oil, just as an example, and depending who was nearest and which storehouse was nearest, this one would be used. So the storehouses were in different locations, and they had one joint responsibility and jurisdiction. The distribution was done at distribution point by local commune commissioners, and the ones from Caritas worked, also, at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This may be a good time for us break, and -- it's our general time, Mr. President, for our break, and then we could go to the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] absolutely. We are going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Stringer, are you about to tell me that you will not be leading this witness during your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, actually, I want to inform the Trial Chamber and the parties of two things which I should have said during the previous session today. The first is to introduce the Trial Chamber to Mr. Ignacio Gomez who as a legal intern with the Office of the Prosector has assisted in our preparation for this witness; and the second was to inform the Trial Chamber that the cross-examination will be conducted by my colleague, Mr. Longone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I have a fourth oral decision which I wish to hand down. This will be very brief. This will be the last decision, I hope. On the 16th of October, 2008, the Trial Chamber has decided to deduct from the Petkovic Defence the time it had taken up when during the cross-examination of Witness Mirko Zelenika. It had addressed topics that had not been addressed during the examination-in-chief of the witness in question. On the same day, the Petkovic Defence asked the Trial Chamber to motivate its decision in order to be able to hand down a decision as soon as possible. The Trial Chamber would like the Prosecution to respond to this motion and to respond on the second argument in particular put forward by the Petkovic Defence. According to the Petkovic Defence, the procedure whereby time is deducted when a particular Defence team addresses topics -- or new topics during the cross-examination of a witness [no interpretation] -- from which time is deducted -- let me read the last paragraph again. Indeed, according to the Petkovic Defence, the procedure whereby time is deducted from one of the Defence teams when it addresses new topics during cross-examination of a witness by [as interpreted] another team of the Defence, this would be unfair given what is applied to the Prosecution. The Prosecution should reply if it so wishes by the 21st of October, 2008, at the latest. Mr. Stringer, could you look into this and respond, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A small observation on the translation. On line 8: "During cross-examination of a witness of another team," not "by another team." What is meant is "the witness of another team."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just thinking quickly, we are in the process of preparing a written submission that goes to, I think, the related -- some related issues that have been raised which relate to scope of cross-examination by the Prosecution and whether documents can be put to Defence witnesses during cross-examination by the Prosecution if those exhibits were not included on the Rule 65 ter list of the Prosecution that was filed some years ago, and I'm just wondering whether it might be best for us to introduce this additional topic in our written submissions which are already being prepared in that they are somewhat related to the issue of cross-examination and -- as between the different parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, the Trial Chamber feels that it is better to separate these topics. Mrs. Alaburic raised a very specific issue, and what you have just said is a much broader topic. Now, as regards the specific issue mentioned by Mrs. Alaburic, we would like you to respond by tomorrow at the latest so that the Trial Chamber can hand down its decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just to clarify. Mr. President, does the Trial Chamber want from the Prosecution a written submission on that or an oral statement of what our position is given the shortness of time? I don't know what your preference is. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like you to respond orally tomorrow afternoon. You can tell us orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We will do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. Frankly, I think we should just cut the Gordian knot on that one, just dispense with the rule and just allow the parties to ask whichever questions they wish that are relevant to their cases, but those are my thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, if we could go to the documents. You have your binder there, and we're going to go to the first document. This portion of the documents has been -- it's under Red Cross organisation in general. 1D 02648. If you could look at that document. We see that it's dated 9 October 1991, and if you could please tell us what this decision is all about, keeping in mind that it's before your time, that is, with the -- with the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] It's okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document shows that this gentleman appointed here received a decision from the Secretariat for National Defence to the effect that he is being appointed to the post in the Red Cross organisation of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we can see at the preamble that this deals with the law on All People's Defence, and it talks about a work obligation. So can we conclude that this appointment is based on -- is a work obligation sort of appointment?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to the next document, 1D 02649. This is dated 10 October 1991, and we see the individual who signed it, and here we see a wartime -- this reflects a wartime assignment. Is that somewhat similar?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document preceded the issuance of this decision. This was the list of individuals that received individual decisions. The previous document just showed that each individual received their own decision on appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it if somebody has this sort of wartime assignment they don't have to have another assignment such as being mobilised into the military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. All the individuals who were assigned to work with Red Cross were obliged to respond and carry out the Red Cross activities stipulated in its statute and under its mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And -- fine. I guess what I was trying to say is if they have that assignment, then they cannot be assigned to have a military obligation.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, they couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I am still with the previous document and -- but also, it is connected to the present one, and that document which is the 2648 and also the other documents here, for me it's somehow creating a problem in the way that although there is a reference to the law on All Peoples Defence, et cetera, when the authorities are given the right to name somebody and to work in any capacity; on the other hand, I really feel that if we are speaking about the Red Cross, and since I also used to be connected to the work of the Hungarian Red Cross in those years - in the 1990s, actually - apart from my other functions and work, I would only ask the witness how and which way the independence of the Red Cross at that time were regarded by the authorities, and was there an authority - Red Cross authority, I mean - which was responsible, also, for ensuring the independence and, of course, the cooperation at the same time of the local Red Cross authorities with the authorities of the municipality, which is my question to the witness: How the structure of the Red Cross has been in a way helped, on the one hand, by the municipal authorities, but on the other, that their independence was also -- or should have been upheld at the same time, in my view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] Since according to the statute the Red Cross is an institution that aids the authorities in carrying out the tasks relative to its mandate, the people who were not able-bodied for military service and had information about how the Red Cross operated were under these orders assigned to help the Red Cross in its activities. Therefore, these people were not the only members of the Red Cross organisation, but in the event of war or any natural disaster they were compelled to report to the Red Cross and work for them, which happened, indeed, in this case, in this particular case of this gentleman and this list. These were the people that I found at the Red Cross in addition to the secretary of the Red Cross who was there according to the preconceived establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like only to say that, of course, this part of your answer is satisfactory, and I see the point, your point, as well. My second question was - and now I reformulate it - that in your view the independence of the work of the Red Cross in Mostar, and of course, let us say that in those circumstances in other municipalities, had been ensured as an independent one in your judgement? And if the answer is yes, which kind of methods were used to have your independence upheld? Of course, at the same time you had to cooperate with the authorities. There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Red Cross's independence is ensured through the bodies that were established in order to monitor the work and the functionality of the Red Cross. Each Red Cross had its own assembly, its presidency, and its working bodies that were directly involved in carrying out the Red Cross activities and, also, the staff on the ground who were at disposal as volunteers for the purposes of implementing the Red Cross mandate. Cooperation with the authorities went as far as we had contact points or common ground in social welfare issues where we cooperated with social welfare institutions, hospitals, and other medical institutions. So these were our joint activities in this specific area. The delivery of humanitarian aid, as well, and its distribution requested and required certain customs, permissions, and other permits; and therefore, we had to cooperate with institutions that issued these permits. We also had coordinated actions with the police if a convoy needed protection or if certain goods had to be secured or protected from theft or any similar situation. So in all the situations where we had certain needs and requirements for the protection from the authorities, we sought this protection. And on the other hand, the authorities only asked us to do what was within our remit and our mandate and created possibilities for us to do the best job we could through certain forms of aid like covering the fuel costs or other minor administrative issues that were able to provide for us and which we were not able to get from donations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your explanation, Mr. Simunovic. That is now clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're very welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just as a follow-up, to your understanding did the Red Cross -- was the Red Cross ever ordered to do anything by the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. A little bit more specific: We understand that there were a list of people that were the recipients of aid, and we'll see that there's also a certain criteria as far as what sort of aid, the amounts of aid to be provided to the recipients. With respect to that aspect of your work, did the municipality, the authorities in any way try to influence who should be on the list, how much aid they should be given, or anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, since the record of the people in need of aid were made up by professional services of the municipality and the Social Services on the ground; and based on these records and the information about the overall number of potential users, we were involved in other activities, as well, not only humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We decided how we were going to operate and what the scope of our aid was going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could look at the next -- the next document, which is 1D 02650. And if you could sort of help us out here a little bit. And again, it's in connection with the previous questions. What is this document, and what does it reflect?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: This document is linked to the previous document. We see these people here, and information was to be entered into the military booklets saying that these persons were available to the Red Cross, and there needed to be a Red Cross stamp on this for the other part to be verified, as well, not just the signature but also the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, going back to the question that was asked by His Honour, if we look on page 2 of this list under number 1, "manager of the professional service secretary." Do you see it? And we see that this is a reserve officer, and it's Omer Katica -- or Arif Katica. Is that it? Arif, because Omer would be his father. Do you see the name?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And who was that individual?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: This was the secretary of the Red Cross. It is precisely pursuant to this request that he was appointed secretary of the Red Cross under his war assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let's go on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have even two questions. Sorry, Mr. Karnavas. First, Witness, in the list a number of numbers are crossed out, and others are encircled. Number 1 is crossed out. Do you know what this means? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Persons whose names are circled were professionally involved with the Red Cross before the war. And the persons whose names are crossed out were in charge of certain fields of activity. For example, there was a non-professional commission including the persons who operated on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. I will not insist on this. I would like to go back to the answer of yours that is recorded on page 45, in lines 14, 15, where you said -- 13 to 15, where you said that the records of the people in need of aid were made up by professional services of the municipality and the social services on the ground. This was in connection with the independence. Now, did you - the Red Cross, Mostar Red Cross - did you in any way control whether these lists were adequate, or did you take them at face value and act on that basis without asking any further questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we had a Red Cross commissioner for each municipality -- or rather, for each local commune, and this person at each of the local communes knew exactly what these persons were and what their status was. Therefore, any report from the social work centre had -- or rather, the Red Cross people had insight into these statuses and the people who worked there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is the first question I put to you: On looking at number 3, Dr. Fazlibegovic, born in 1953. Can you confirm that this was a physician who was dealing with medical problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is the son, as I can read, of Mehmed or Ahmed Emir. Is he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. He's Ahmed's son. Father's names are in the brackets here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This Muslim who was a doctor worked for the Red Cross in Mostar. For the entire period of the war or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He worked at the Mostar hospital. As for his work with the Red Cross, he monitored activities related to the administration of first aid and other activities being monitored by him or other activities pursued by the Red Cross. He was not a Red Cross employee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that he worked at the hospital. You told us that there were two hospitals, one hospital in West Mostar and one hospital in East Mostar. Which hospital was he working in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one hospital in Mostar, and he worked with that hospital. And he still works there, as a matter of fact; and today, it's in West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, right, May, June, July, August 1993, where was this doctor? Was he in West Mostar, in East Mostar? Where was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] West. West.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During this period May, June, July, August, September, October, November 1993, did he attend the Red Cross meetings? Was he working for the Red Cross in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't with the Red Cross at the time, I. He was an activist. He was a volunteer with the Red Cross, but he was an employee of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And as I understand it, at that time - correct me if I'm wrong - as I understood you, at that time there was only one hospital in Mostar. Is that correct? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you said that this list is of people -- of individuals working with the Red Cross before you arrived. Do they continue to work when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: All those actively involved with the Red Cross continued to work there even following my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02653. This is May 20th, 1992. Again, it's prior to your arrival, but here if we look at this document it's -- it purports to -- it's from a -- these are minutes of a meeting of the founding of a regional Red Cross, and here we see Mostar under Group I, number 7. When you started working with the Red Cross and throughout your tenure with the Red Cross, can you tell us whether this regional organisation worked in a manner in which these minutes reflect?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The regional Red Cross was working as a unified organisation made up of the 38 municipal organisations. No division such as this Groups I, II, and III as reflected here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in reality, this was never implemented?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
