utterances.text: Okay. If we look at 1D 02652. This is the first meeting of staff of the regional Red Cross. This is seven days later. It's 27 May 1992. If we look at that, and again, I understand this is before your time, but I want to draw your attention first, if you look under item number 2, that a Mr. Branko Leko from Posusje was proposed and unanimously elected. Can you tell us whether that was in fact the case, that Mr. Leko was elected, I guess, as the regional president?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what role did he play as the regional president during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: He was a very cooperative and productive person. He was also the initiator as the chairman of this body of meetings, coordination meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me -- let's look at item number 3. It says here, because this will come up if I don't raise it, that there was a controversial debate, a long and controversial debate on the proposal of Grude and Livno; and it was voted that Grude should be chosen as the temporary seat of the regional Red Cross. Can you tell us whether you later on came to know what the controversy was all about, why Grude versus Livno?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what I learnt at a later stage, Grude was chosen for two reasons, one having to do directly with the position of the chief secretary, with the staff, Mr. Bozo Vukoja [phoen], who was at the same time the executive manager of the Grude Red Cross; the other having to do with the possibility of communicating because Livno was quite far away in relation to most of the municipalities that made up the Red Cross, and communication was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Again, I'm going to ask you to speak slowly. It doesn't help if you speak fast and then pause. So you have to sort of, like, pace it.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then still pause but not too long.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're welcome. 1D 02655. You spoke of a statute. We see this is May 1992, and this is the statute of the regional Red Cross. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When I started working with the Mostar Red Cross, I had occasion to look at this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, again, going back to what the question was, I'm trying to figure out if I understood the question that was posed from the Bench. If we look at Article 2, it talks about voluntary humanitarian organisation of citizens; and again, we went back and we saw that this was a document with respect to the assignment, and it was as if the person being assigned was actually being ordered as a work obligation. Is there any conflict in that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So how could it be -- how could it be a voluntary and independent organisation if at the same time somebody's being ordered to perform work at the Red Cross due to their war assignment?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Red Cross is an organisation whose scope is broader than just working within the working organ of the Red Cross where people actually work if you take the municipal organisations, the basic organisations based across schools and municipalities, so the Red Cross stretches far and wide across each and every one of these municipalities on a voluntary basis, on the basis of spreading humanitarian and other mandates. The institution itself, because it performs its very peculiar tasks in keeping with the Geneva Conventions and other protocols and agreements as stated in Article 2, is a humanitarian organisation of citizens which is an organisation of special social interest. That's line 3 in Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. If we could look at Article 8, we see a purpose of work under Article 8, and then again, we see a basic pragmatic task under Article 9. I take it, having looked at Articles 8 and 9, can you tell us whether the same purpose of work and the same basic pragmatic tasks were also part of the mandate of the Mostar municipal or any municipal Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, because these commitments and the purpose of activity was something that followed from the international conventions. One of the organisations could not meet all of the requirements, but in every statute the commitment was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to Article 9 very briefly and we look at the second to last -- the penultimate bullet point, if you will, it says: "To collect, organise, keep, and provide the data on victims of armed conflicts and mass adversities and carry out other activities of tracing service." Can you tell us whether this was part of the mandate being carried out by the Mostar municipal Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Mostar Red Cross was gathering information on victims. It was also gathering information on accidents. It was also mediating with the international committee in terms of exchanging information on people who had been separated. It was also helping reunite families and missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02654. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a follow-up question. These tasks, Witness, are the same tasks basically that are the tasks of the municipal Red Cross; is that correct? There is no basic difference. That certain task would be exclusively on the regional level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the statute of the regional Red Cross was the one that other statutes for municipal organisations were based on. Every municipal organisation was under an obligation to perform operative work on the ground and to perform these very duties and commitments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I don't want to get ahead of myself because we will see a document later on which is the statute for the Mostar municipality, but that's dated November 1993. But at that time, was there a local statute for the Mostar municipality or other municipalities that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The Mostar Red Cross never worked without a statute that applied. The Red Cross statute was there, and it was based on principles of the international movement. The statute of the Mostar Red Cross was based on the Bosnia and Herzegovina Red Cross statute, the one that applied at the time. When the regional Red Cross was established, given the fact that Mostar was part of this regional Red Cross, we based our statute on the regional Red Cross statute, which itself, if you look at the title and introduction, was consistent with the BH Red Cross statute. If you look at the preamble to this statute, it invokes the BH Red Cross statute, if you look at the conclusions from the regional Red Cross Assembly of establishment for further work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you again to please speak a little slower so that the translators are not overtaxed because they are trying their level best to be as accurate as possible. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02654, and everyone should have been provided with the corrected version of this document, the corrected translated version of it, we see this is dated 4 June 1992. We see at the bottom the gentleman that we made reference to earlier, Branko Leko, and at the very first paragraph, it says: "Due to the broken communications with the headquarters of this humanitarian organisation in Sarajevo and war-affected areas in our republic, municipal organisations of the Red Cross in the Croatian cantonal areas have joined together into a regional association of the Red Cross of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna with the headquarters in Grude." My one question is: Knowing that you didn't join the Red Cross until a few -- a couple weeks later, nonetheless, can you tell us whether, indeed, this is accurate, that is at that time the communications were broken between the headquarters -- the headquarters in Sarajevo and, say, other places such as Mostar municipality? And this is, again, concerning the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were not able to communicate with Sarajevo at the time I arrived and for the following 20-odd days. We were unable to communicate with the headquarters of the International Red Cross -- of the BH Red Cross in Sarajevo, and this situation continued for quite a long time afterwards given the situation that prevailed in Sarajevo. In some cases, to do with some requests we used ham radio operators to establish communication, but that was the only line of communication that was open to us whenever we were doing our best to assist a particular person and, of course, messages from the international committee because those were -- always arrived in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. If we go on to the next document 1D 02434. If you could please look at it. And again, this pre-dated your arrival, so my first question would be: At the time that you did start working and thereafter with the Red Cross of the Mostar municipality, did you become acquainted with the agreements that are contained in this particular exhibit, 1D 02434?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a chance to look at this document at the time, but I am familiar with the Red Cross mandate through brochures, leaflets and documents that were forwarded to us by the international committee. I look at what this document reflects, which is a document that I saw at a later stage, and it reflects verbatim the provisions of the Geneva Conventions and the mandate of the international committee, as well as that of International Red Cross branches at a local or national level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at concretely page 4, for instance, where at the bottom of the page we see a section called "Beneficiaries and types of assistance." If you go on to page -- the bottom of page 4 and on to page 5, we see different criteria. Can you tell us whether this was being followed in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: This was the prescribed minimum, prescribed by the International Red Cross committee for aid in the eventuality of disasters and catastrophes, and then they list all the various population groups or categories. If there was any aid that was available in quantities that were sufficient for those in need, then we were able to distribute aid to this extent. If not, then more time would be granted for the distribution process itself or between two rounds of distribution or shipments, if you like, which gave us a chance to put together a package that was realistic and that met these requirements because any other sort of distribution or breakdown or division would have been insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we're going to cover that in greater detail later on. I just wanted to get that bit information at this point. Now, if we could go on to the next document, 1D 02660. This is the statute of the Mostar municipal organisation of the Red Cross dated November 1993, and we see President Marinko Simunovic. That's you, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you are familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I guess it begs the question if the regional statute that we saw earlier was -- was dated May 1992, why did it take so long - November 1993 - for there to be a statute for the Mostar municipal Red Cross? And be very brief about it.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was difficult to convene the Red Cross Assembly during the actual war. That's one of the reasons. Under the statute, only an Assembly can amended the statutes or adopt new phrasing, a piece of new phrasing for the statute. Secondly, we had a statute that actually applied, and this allowed us to undertake any activity in terms of our reaction when it came to the fundamental task of the Red Cross, which was to provide various forms of aid. Therefore, the late adoption of this statute - if I may put it that way - was an excuse for our statute to be brought in line with the Red Cross statute at the national level, the BH Red Cross statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- and if we look at Article 7 and Article 8, going back to Judge Trechsel's question, we see in Article 7 the goals and activities; in Article 8, the main programme goals. I take it these were the actual activities that were being carried out even prior to the adoption of this statute; is that correct? Based on your previous answer, that is.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And before we leave this document, let me just ask you one general question. During that period of time, as I understand it from your testimony earlier, the ICRC were there and, of course, UNHCR. Were there ever any complaints to your knowledge -- were there any complaints to your knowledge that the Red Cross of the Mostar municipality was not carrying out its activities properly?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was even quite the opposite. The Red Cross of Mostar was commended for the way it operated and how it implemented the required mandate, and precisely for those reasons we were recognised as a very reliable, transparent and good partner for receipt and distribution of humanitarian aid on the one hand and as a good partner of the ICRC and other organisations when it comes to other forms of activities that the Red Cross was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We go on to the next document, 1D 02661, and this is the last document in this segment. This is the Law on the Red Cross of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It's dated -- I believe it's November 1994 -- October 1994. Why was it necessary to pass this law, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if we refer to what was said before, the Red Cross is an aiding organisation which provides help to the authorities in pursuing the goals and programme tasks, then we in the Red Cross were very keen on regulate our activities in a legal way and thereby make it possible for us to be better and more efficient in our work. We also wanted to resolve the question of cooperation with the government institutions at all levels to resolve the issue of functioning and financing of the Red Cross and to solve certain problems relating to responsibility in working for the Red Cross and by the Red Cross and the mandate that it was supposed to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we go on to the next segment. Unless there are any questions, we'll go on to the next topic which deals with, in general, we call it refugee status, but we will be dealing with these sorts of issues, refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have just seen a whole series of documents that show us how the Mostar Red Cross was put in place at the level of the municipality but also at regional level, and as I understood it, you were the president of the Red Cross in Mostar. Earlier on, we mentioned the ICRC. Did you have any contacts with the International Committee of the Red Cross, and if so, who were you in permanent contact with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had contacts with the ICRC and with the delegates of the ICRC who were in charge of cooperation in our area, either through meetings and conversations on our premises or through meetings in their offices that were in various locations both in Mostar and outside of Mostar. It all depended on what they wanted to do and how they organised things. The initial contact I personally had with the ICRC in Split. Late Mostar offices and field offices were established. And during intense fighting in 1993, they relocated their offices to Medjugorje. After that, they came back to Mostar again, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give us the names of your counterparts, the usual ones, the ones that were in Medjugorje and the one who moved to Mostar? Could you give us some names, professional contacts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have to look at my journal, and that would take some time. I do remember, though, some persons, some individuals. For example, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Excuse me. Because of the sensitivity, we may need to do this in closed session, as I understand it. You know, this is the type of organisation that doesn't like to either participate in these sorts of events, and so I don't want to compromise -- I mean, I don't care one way or the other, but they certainly won't come and testify in court because they wish to maintain their neutrality, so that's the only reason. But I have no objection one way or the other, but I'm just bringing it to the Court's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but you do not have any specific names, do you? Because you said you had to look into your documents. So I don't think it's even worth going into private session since you can't give me any names. The thing that interested me was to know whether you had any contacts, and you said you did. That's the main thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, let me just pick up where you left off a little bit. You had indicated -- the question was whether you had contact with the ICRC, and then you mention that at one point in May they moved to Medjugorje, correct? Or you just said that. Now --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it -- and I'll just get ahead of the story at this point. As I understand it, at some point you were asked to go to the Heliodrom on or about May 9, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for humanitarian reasons and providing relief to the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. We're going to go step by step. There's nothing to be alarmed by. Can you please describe to us, of course, now, why did you go there and what exactly did you do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The only reasons for us going there was to find a way and to have an insight into the prevailing situation and to find a way of providing help to the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you here. Did you go -- volunteer and go on your own, or were you asked to go there? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, upon my arrival and my joining the Red Cross of Mostar, I found - I have to say that - a devastated Red Cross, particularly the premises where it was housed, because our offices were 200 metres from the front line at the time where combat operations were ongoing. Then I learned what actually had happened, and that is that a certain number of people were put up that night at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I immediately got in my car and went to the site to see what it was all about. With me was my assistant for humanitarian issues. I wanted to see if there was anyone I can talk to and how I could help these people because I learned that there was a large number of civilians there. And those are precisely the category that we had been providing help to and who were the beneficiaries of our aid. I went back to the warehouse, see what the situation was and established a channel for providing aid to the extent that we were capable of doing. We provide aid in food, toiletries, and all other items that were available on stock. However, at the time I have to say we did not have sufficient quantities of goods because the inflows from other humanitarian organisations were considerably reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're going to talk about that period and what was available as far as resources to distribute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. You had started off by asking about Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And he hasn't answered. Yeah. Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I haven't moved on. I mean, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought you were going further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, I -- he mentioned something about -- there was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I've heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My first question now is, staying with the Heliodrom, was somebody coordinating this effort that you were involved in, that is assisting and providing aid? Was anybody on that end working with you or coordinating these efforts?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I had contact with the chief logistical officer of this institution and these facilities, as well as with people who were working with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness, because you're jumping one step, skipping one step, because this topic of the Heliodrom is an important one, as you know well. I've listened to you carefully so far, and I understood that together with a colleague of yours, you got on board a vehicle and you drove to the Heliodrom in order to assess the situation. That's what you said, isn't it? When you got there -- well, is there the Red Cross sign on the car, or was it a civilian car? And when you got to the Heliodrom, whom did you see? What did that person tell you? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I drove in a car that had the Red Cross markings, and that was always my practice, to use the vehicles with the Red Cross sign. At the gate of Heliodrom, we were allowed to pass through once they saw the Red Cross sign. I reached the building where the military command was. I was familiar with this area because that is where I was born. I asked if there's anyone I can talk to about the humanitarian aid for the people who were being kept there. I met with the person who was in charge of logistics in military terms, and I assessed the needs with this person and assessed the quantities that we were able to provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that nobody prevented you from doing your work. Could you feel there was some resistance, because when one sees the Red Cross arrive, that may arise -- that may cause problems sometimes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have such problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm sure there will be more questions from the Bench on this. Just let me get in a question or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Aside from providing humanitarian aid as you just described, did you at any point in time do an inspection of the premises to see the conditions of the premises and the condition of the people, whether they were sufficiently being taken care of? Did you do any of that? And that's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are we still talking about Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. We haven't left it. You'll know when we leave Heliodrom. We're going to be there for a while.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Okay. [Interpretation] I didn't carry out any detailed inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Because the office where we had a meeting was on the ground floor. I thought that I had to respond quickly. I left this office after an hour at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Excuse me. You just told the President of the -- of the Trial Chamber that you could come and go. Everybody respected you. They saw that you were with the Red Cross. Why did you not walk around and inspect the premises at some point to see how those people that were there, how they were being kept, you know, whether they had sufficient facilities, the food. Did you do any of that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one of the reasons that we didn't have an opportunity to do that was because the ICRC came and they undertook to assess the condition in which the people were being kept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, did you ever -- was that part of the mandate as far as you know, the mandate of the Mostar municipality or any municipality, that is, to inspect places?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: If these were officially pronounced as prisons, then the local Red Crosses did not have the mandate to do any inventory or inspection of the persons kept on such premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about for tracing purposes? Were any efforts made, for instance, in providing forms for folks to fill out if they wanted to locate missing family members or friends? Was any of that done by -- by you or your staff during that period?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: On that site, the ICRC also undertook all activities in this regard. They distributed the messages, and they took over the written messages that actually came from that site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us, to what extent did you provide humanitarian assistance? You said you went back, you looked for it. Was it one day, two days? What sort of stuff did you bring back to this location?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We first and foremost provided toiletries and food that could be cooked on the premises or in the kitchen where food was being prepared for the staff on the site, and we also took a number of blankets and mattresses and other items that we had available and that could have facilitated this improvised accommodation of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there's something I'm finding difficult to understand. The authority of your organisation and the ICRC, if I am to understand your answers just provided to Mr. Karnavas, you were in charge of toiletries, food, and mattresses, and the ICRC had to handle all the rest? What are the different competencies of the ICRC and your body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The mandate of the ICRC with regard to persons who are incarcerated was to keep records and to assess the situation and to distribute messages and later on convey these messages to the recipients. This is the usual mandate of the ICRC in a situation where you have people in incarceration. Our Red Cross, on the other hand, in this particular case was involved only in the humanitarian aspect of the situation, that is, the provision of the necessary aid for these people such as food, toiletries, and items relating to their accommodation conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand better. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could go to the documents, going back to the documents, and I'm going to first refer you to 1D 00596. And here, this is 25 July 1992. It's a conclusion on the introduction of refugee files or -- I believe it should say cards, who come to Mostar municipality. And if we look at under Article 2, it talks about the office for Social Welfare, Health Care and Refugees of the Mostar Municipality, of the Mostar Municipal Croatian Defence Council. Can you tell us what this is all about? What are they talking about when they say refugee cards or files, and are you familiar with this particular office, the office for social welfare?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically, this document is something that I found later at the Red Cross, and I knew that it had been issued. This document refers to the previous lists compiled at various locations of the expellees and refugees, and this constitutes an effort to bring some order to these records containing the names of the people who arrived to the municipality of Mostar from other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the office for social welfare, were you familiar with this particular office, and if so, how? Very quickly, please, because we really do need to move on.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This office was functioning as part of municipal authorities in Mostar, and it has offices in charge for all these domains relating to general social welfare issue and protection as well as the refugees in Mostar municipalities. This office employed professionals, and it is only logical to expect that these professionals would be entrusted with taking care of issuing cards or establishing files relating to these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next document, 1D 00623. These are the "rules on protecting refugees and displaced persons in Mostar municipality," and this is September 16, 1992. Are you familiar with this -- this document, and could you please tell us how so?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document. It essentially contains an effort to regulate the situation pertaining to the expellees and refugees and expellees in Mostar on various levels, that is to say with regard to their status, their rights, their protection and, generally speaking, records relating to them. This document also indicates or -- that there was a need to cooperate with the Red Cross and other humanitarian organisations. So I was fully aware of the contents of this document and, believe me, I was glad that this document had been issued because there was chaos in terms of seeking aid. People would go from one location to another exerting pressure on humanitarian organisations, on social welfare institutions. They tried to gather as much aid as possible without valid arguments, and that was a good opportunity to bring some order in this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you look at the next document and -- actually, the next two documents are very similar. 1D 02759 and -- and of course, the next one, 1D 02761. We see these are -- these are family cards. Are you familiar with these documents?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you just very briefly tell us what these documents are. What is a family card, and how does it work?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The family card, as you can see here, was something that each family -- after an analysis was made by professionals and in the presence of representatives of humanitarian organisations, it was established that they are eligible to receive humanitarian aid, and this kind of card was then subsequently issued to them in order to facilitate the registration or the entry of dates when they received aid, including the type of aid received, and this card had to be verified or certified to the effect that this person and his or her family, at the time when they applied for aid, were eligible to receive it. In other words, all the individuals in local communes who needed aid had either a family card, if they were heads of the household, or individual cards for those who didn't have families and was deemed to be a valid beneficiary. On the front page, top side, you can see that this card is valid and each subsequent date is another verification of the fact that the carrier or the holder of this card is the recipient of aid. On the second page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: It's not shown on the screen, so I'm waiting. Page 2, if you look at the left-hand column, you have the type of aid that was provided to this person or family. You have the date, which means that this was when the aid reached the family or the person. I do have to admit that column 2 and column 3 are somewhat clumsy, and you see that the dates were copied from column 3 back to column 2 on the day when aid was redistributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 00754, and this is a document -- we've seen this before. This is a decision. It's dated 15th of April, 1993, and it's a decision governing the rights granted to refugees, expelled persons, and internally displaced persons. And we can look -- if we look at Article I, we see that there's an exclusion to certain persons that are within the age of 17 to 60 and women 17 to 55, and ultimately we'll see another document where this was amended, so it's 18 as opposed to 17. Were you familiar with this decision at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we talk about the decision, could you kindly explain to us what the situation was like in Mostar, you having been there, living there, and then working very closely and distributing humanitarian aid? Can you please tell us what the situation was like? And in particular, we're concerned about expelled persons, refugees, internally displaced, the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as for the situation in the period leading up to this decision and right after, there were almost 30.000 beneficiaries of humanitarian aid living in Mostar, all because of different reasons. To provide sufficient aid for such large numbers of people enjoying the status of displaced persons or refugees was an enormous endeavour. Another thing we were facing was that the aid which had been more plentiful before now merely continued to trickle in to the Red Cross; and according to our records, the situation was the same in other humanitarian organisations whose work we coordinated, as I explained before. Another problem that occurred was people becoming double beneficiaries of humanitarian aid, people living at two different locations. That is why you see paragraph II in this decision, indicating that internally displaced persons must go back to wherever they can in Mostar municipality in order to avail themselves of their right to receive humanitarian aid in one location alone. Likewise, men of military age. If you look at paragraph I, you can see that. Men of military age were busy in their military units, and they weren't classified as being in need of various forms of aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at also Article IV. Here, it says: "Pursuant to Items I, II, and III herein, internally displaced persons, expelled persons, or refugees put up in education facilities shall be relocated to other collective accommodation facilities for expelled persons..." and so on. Can you please explain to us why this would have been necessary, this Article, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I know that schools were used to house refugee centres. I know that the idea was to have the schools back up and running and for the construction to continue. It was for this reason that one tried to have these people who were occupying schools moved to other buildings, or if these were internally displaced people, to be moved back to whichever areas were available to them in order to make the schools available again for teaching to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let's look at 1D 01083, and let's see what Jablanica does a few weeks earlier, 19 March 1993. Perhaps we could draw some comparisons. And here, it says: "Until further notice, the Red Cross shall issue refugee cards with temporary residence to refugees and displaced persons who are not military conscripts and arrive in Jablanica municipality after this Presidency's order ..." So looking at Article I and looking at the previous decision, are there any similarities or dissimilarities in what is happening in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: It's quite obvious that there are similarities, the idea being that men of military age should be taken off the humanitarian aid distribution lists. Likewise, if you look at paragraph II, the idea is to safeguard buildings in which schools could continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- to operate. So the reasons are very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [In English] Now it's time for the break. [Interpretation] We will have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you have used one hour and 27 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to have to -- we need to get through one more document, actually, with this chapter. There are two in the binders, in this particular chapter, and this is -- we'll look at P 02151, and again, keeping in mind the decision of April 15, that is 1D 00754, which was then amended on the 29th of April, which is P 02140. But let's look at this conclusion, P 02151. This is from Merhamet. First, do you know the gentleman by the name of Izet Sahovic? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I still work with him. He's deputy manager of the Mostar airport, and we work together on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, and this document is dated 30th of April, 1993, and in this document it makes reference to the previous ones that we talked about, the decision of 15 April 1993. My first question is, were you aware of this particular conclusion at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Not this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand -- I want you to look at now 1D 02813. Do you have it there? It should be in your binder. 1D 02813. That's the very next document. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And as I understand it, you have your diary with you, the entire diary back then?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The entire diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this was a diary that you -- you allowed us to copy and which, also, you allowed us to provide to the rest of the parties, including the Prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: One proviso though. What I see on the screen is not exactly what the page contains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- let me show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If the usher could please assist us here and give this to the gentleman. I'm told that we need to put the number on the e-court, or you could put it on ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the document, but what I see here on the screen is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just -- please work with me because I'm under a tight schedule, and all these little delays are valuable time -- is valuable time lost. What do your notes reflect?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: My notes reflect one of the meetings with the UNHCR on the 30th of April, 1993, with members of the Caritas attending, the Red Crescent, Merhamet, the Red Cross, and other humans organisations that were part of the coordination committee for the reception and distribution of humanitarian aid in Mostar municipality. What was discussed at the meeting was the situation regarding food shipments, the shortage of food in the UNHCR system, and other problems to do with the arrival of humanitarian aid. It was also concluded that throughout that period there were 30.000 beneficiaries of humanitarian aid throughout Mostar municipality. Likewise, if you go further down you see that new refugees are arriving from Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: If you turn the page, you see on page 2, child care is referred to there, and then one debated the change in the status of refugees and displaced persons, and this had to do with the aforementioned decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: My own remark about this was that the decision also had to do with the overall quantities of food available. Earlier on, we stated the other reasons for the decision to be adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at that point in time, since we see that Merhamet was present, did they take a position or did the -- did the decision of 15 of April come up?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in the sense of the previous document what their reaction would be. That wasn't something that would actually stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that wasn't brought up at the meeting on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And again, just to be clear, this meeting, by looking at those who were participating, are these the participants of this coordinating committee?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, if we go on to the next chapter which ties in a little bit with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. One follow-up question. I'm looking at your handwritten notes. They are about a meeting with the UNHCR, with Caritas, and Merhamet. I'm interested in Merhamet. At that meeting, who was the Merhamet representative? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the representative of Merhamet at most of these meetings was Mr. Izet Sahovic. The Merhamet office, the Mostar Merhamet, was in the same building as the Red Cross. We passed through the same door every day to gain access to the building, and he was at most of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So that's on the 30th of April, ten days away from the 9th of May, 1993. What was the mood of the Merhamet representative? Did he think that the situation was caused by a generalised conflict, or did he blame the HVO? What was his personal point of view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were dealing with humanitarian issues and nothing else. We were only considering the amounts of humanitarian aid available to us. Was it sufficient? Was it possible to distribute the quantities that we had? We never went any deeper into the relations that you mentioned except in as far as it concerned humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you well, you were exclusively interested in the consequences of the situation, not in the causes of it together with the other participants. You were only speaking about the consequences. You did not deal with the causes thereof.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. We did not. We talked about what we had to do if the quantities of food decreased and the number of persons to be fed increased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: After this particular meeting, did Merhamet continue to -- to show up at these coordinating committee meetings and participate?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The next meeting was attended by people from Merhamet on the 4th of May, and then they stopped coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- okay. When was the next meeting in May? What date?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We have it on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when did they start -- when did they start showing up again to meetings, if they ever did?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Early in June. I can't remember the exact date, but it's somewhere in my notes. It was between the 12th and the 15th of June. There was a regular meeting that was held during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are a few questions. Wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to ask a question. You made a reference a few minutes ago to the Red Cross and also to the -- to Crescent Rouge. That is mainly that part of the International Red Cross -- Red Crescent movement which are from the Muslim States. I wonder if when you mentioned Crescent Rouge, Red Crescent, if you had in mind let's say the Crescent Rouge, Red Crescent, from Turkey or from other countries, and have they been there active in that part of Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The organisation was established, the Red Crescent, at the municipal level in Mostar. It actively took part in the work of the coordinating committee despite the fact that you can't have two organisations with two different coats of arms, as it were, active in one country. We had an opportunity to get the maximum amount of aid, so we went along with this, for this organisation to continue its work because all they were doing was about humanitarian work. Their participants were actively involved in all of the coordination meetings held by the coordinating committee. They were highly cooperative. They provided a lot of information. They helped with the situation, and they made a number -- a significant number of donations. One can assume that they got the aid that they provided to us from countries under the sign of the Red Crescent, but this is something that can be easily checked if you go back to their records. I'm not privy to any detail about their sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Simunovic, although I would have liked to know if that organisation as you just explained was a grassroots organisation only in Mostar, or was it in a way connected to national -- other national branches like -- let's say in Sarajevo or any other place; because as we all know, the Red Crescent and the movement is in a way also international as such, that is the federation of the national societies of Red Cross and Red Crescent. So my question was mainly directed to the fact if they had any international relationship or they were only acting in the field of -- rather, not national but only local levels. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they operated in several municipalities across Bosnia and Herzegovina. Their structure was not a closed one in terms of hierarchy. They operated locally across local communes, but there were some missions through activities well known to me because I participated in the process of establishing the Red Cross of the federation and the society of the Red Cross at the federal level to start setting up a national structure of the Red Crescent in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which at the same time as you suggested was not possible because in one country you can only have one symbol and one society. Later on when the situation normalised, we discussed this problem, and we as the Red Cross -- or rather, there were no prerequisites in place for a national form of the Red Crescent to be established since the BH Red Cross had already had a tradition of some 80 years, and the international movement did not order dual or double signs or symbols or two such societies in one country. So you're quite right. They didn't have the structures, but I was in those bodies and structures establishing the Red Cross and international recognition. But at this point in time, there were no problems for them being the institution that they were to get humanitarian aid because that was in everyone's best interest, and that was a top priority at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when there was the federal republic, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the time was there both the Red Cross and the Red Crescent, or was there only the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the Red Cross, which had been part of the Red Cross of Yugoslavia; but the way it was structured, now there was only one institution, Red Cross - "kriz" or "krst" - because of the dual use of that word in the various variants of the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to the structure of the Red Crescent, for instance, in Mostar, what time did they show up?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, Your Honour. If we look at document 1D 00643, which is in the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'll find the answer in that document. Maybe I was ahead of myself. Sorry, Mr. Karnavas. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go back -- now I want to go to your report, which is 1D 02651. This is your report, is it not? It's dated 23 March 1994, but it's -- it's for the activities of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And as I understand it, in this report there are some charts which may be of some assistance to the previous answers that you gave concerning the availability of humanitarian aid in and around the months of April and May of 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And perhaps if we could look at two charts that might be of some assistance, and it might be easier if we look at the B/C/S version. And the one chart -- I'll read the number at the bottom. It's 1D 510756. That would be -- that would be the first one. Maybe we could pull it up on -- so everyone can see it. And in English, it's 1D 570376. Do you have the chart with you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could please explain this chart to us, what does it mean, and how can we read it? First, what does the title say?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The title reads: "Dynamics of entry of humanitarian aid into municipal Red Cross Mostar in 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Lower down you see the months, and then this vertical column shows the amount in terms of tonnes of humanitarian aid that came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at the months of April and May, we could see how much came to the Red Cross; is that correct? If you look at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. It can be seen clearly. January, February, March, the humanitarian aid arrival was on the wane; and then some more came in in April; and then May, June, July, quite poor in terms of humanitarian aid being received by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document -- the next page, here we see another chart. Perhaps you could help us out on this one. And that would --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that the Red Cross was keeping records, also, for the other organisations that were part of the coordinating committee, in our report we provided an illustration of the overall influx of humanitarian aid in relation to all the organisations that were part of the committee. It clearly shows that in April there was a significant decrease in terms of humanitarian aid coming in, and that was in relation to nearly all the institutions, and in May it was simply insubstantial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. To make sure that I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Your Honours, in the English version, it's 1D 570377.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at this particular chart, this has all of the aid that is coming in to the coordinating body as opposed to the previous one, which just reflected the aid that came into the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it be this amount of aid that would then have to be distributed to everyone who was in need of that humanitarian aid in and around Mostar municipality?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The humanitarian aid that was available in January, February, and March was meant to be distributed, yes, of course. However, nothing arrived; nothing new arrived in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, unfortunately what we don't have, it would appear, we don't have a trend or statistics as to how many refugees were there at the time, right? We don't have this in this --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't keep that kind of record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: But one can cross-reference this to the previous one showing that there were over -- or about 30.000 beneficiaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that was based on the document that we saw that comes out of your diary, 1D 02813. You have to say something because we need to make a record.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't mean to be aggressive, but time is -- and I take it -- let me just ask this question in a non-leading fashion. When were those notes taken that are in your diary? When were the notes taken, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The day it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Contemporaneously?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That goes for every page, of course. Contemporaneously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, sticking with your report, very briefly, again, because we need to move on, if we go on to the last few pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think it's the last two or three pages, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What we see -- and this would be 1D 510764, 765, 766, this is in the original version. We see a -- we see a list, and then we see HRD, which I suspect, it's Croatian dinar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then further down at the bottom and on the next page, we see DEM, and I take it that's Deutschmarks.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At some point we see ITL, and I take it that would be Italian lira?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain to us why you're referencing here the aid in Croatian dinar, Deutschmark, or lira?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm referring to pages 22 to 24 in the English version, Your Honours, for the record and for everyone's benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So why is it in Croatian dinar, Deutschmark, or lira? Could you give us a quick explanation so I can move on.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, each annual report contains a financial report. This is about certain amounts that were indicated in Croatian dinar. That represented our transactions through the clearing house, and at the time the clearing house was doing business in Croatian dinar. The amounts in other currencies were donations from certain countries, and this was reflected in the currency designated. If you look at the title page, you can see that the Mostar Red Cross had an account with the ZAP in Mostar in Croatian dinar and a currency account in the equivalent foreign currency, and this allowed us to receive donations from a variety of sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And that -- that brings me to my next question because we see a giro account. I take it that -- was that for -- well, what was it for, the giro account? What does that reflect?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Every institution registered was obliged to open an appropriate account in order to conduct its business, and quite simply once we applied for registration, we filled out the form and we acted as the other institutions did at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But where are you opening up this account? For some of us who may not know, where is this account located?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which institution?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That was the clearing house --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The payment bureau?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: ZKP?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I can't lead you. That's why I'm trying to get you to give me the answers, but we got there. Now, with respect to the banks - because this may be an issue that the Judges may wish to explore or my colleagues - we see one bank -- or two banks or two accounts, one for foreign currency, one for domestic. Can you tell us, when you joined, when you joined the Red Cross back in July 1992, were these accounts in existence at the time, these bank accounts?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was only the one previously opened with the clearing house, and that was the institution that acted as a service for socially owned institutions and other businesses for internal transactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you mean clearing house, you're talking about the payment bureau?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We just need to be precise. Were banks available at the time? Were they functioning in and around Mostar at the time, do you know, when you joined the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me -- well, yes, in a sense, but how they operated and what problems they were facing, I don't know. All I know is that we used these two accounts for our business transactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02772. This is the next segment. This deals with distribution of humanitarian aid in general, and here we see someone being appointed. Could you please explain what this document is about; and the social welfare centre, what is that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was part of the municipal institutions in Mostar. The social welfare centre operated within this system. This centre worked together with the local community; and at the proposal of a representative of the local commune, they appointed people to coordinate work on the issues relating to this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, what was the function of the local commune concerning the distribution of aid? What was its function?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That was a direct distribution point of humanitarian aid. So in cooperation with the commissioner from the centre and the government commissioner for this particular local commune as well as representatives of international humanitarian organisations, humanitarian aid was first collected from the storehouses of the organisations participating in the coordinating committee, preparing them for distribution, keeping records and cards on the status of beneficiaries, and direct distribution of aid that arrived in this particular local commune and was provided by the coordinating committee, or rather, the organisations operating in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: There was first internal reception, and every time a list for distribution was publicly exposed or made, it was made known to the public which kind of category of population was due to receive aid and at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You're going to have to speak a little slower. So just to make sure that I understand you, at the local commune when there was a distribution to be made, they would publish it so that the community -- the members of the commune, those living in and around would know when the distribution would occur and what was being distributed.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it based on your previous answer, somebody with a card may then be qualified and would go and collect. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to the lists that was publicised so that everyone who came on a certain day would receive the same items. There couldn't have been any differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about if somebody wasn't on the list but they felt that they -- that they needed to collect some humanitarian aid, you know, at that level? Do you know what the procedure would be, if any, for such a person either to get a card or to at least get some -- some aid on the spot?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, basically, according to the adopted rules, a person may apply to acquire the right to aid and to be given a card. In Mostar municipality, there were also soup kitchens established where everyone who felt that they had no other way of getting a meal on a particular day were able to go and get one there, or they could try and just talk to someone and attempt to get aid, but I think that it's happened very seldom for anyone to get any aid unless they had a proper card.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, which brings me to my next question. Who would -- you said they would have to fill out a form to get the card. Would that happen at the commune level, or would it happen at some higher level? Who would make this -- where would the actual form be filled out, and who would be making the decision, at what level?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: These forms were filled out at the local commune. The social welfare centre had their commissioners at the local level, as well as did the humanitarian organisations, and people simply knew who had what status in their community, and that would be confirmed through the issuing of a card, and the social welfare centre had to verify this card.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we go on to the next document, 1D 01328. This is a decision to establish the Coordination Committee for Collection, Reception, and Distribution of Humanitarian Aid. Now, we've already discussed somewhat or you talked about a coordination committee. Is that what this decision is all about, setting up that particular committee?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the foundation for setting up this body; and on the basis of this document, we initiated meetings and launched our activities, agreed how we were going to operate. We prepared, also, documents that would help us monitor the whole activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on -- under Article II, it says: "The committee shall have president and vice-president who shall be elected by the committee members ..." and so on. Do you recall who were the president and vice-president of the coordination committee? Do you recall offhand?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know these names, but I do know that the Red Cross was an administrative and operative support in terms of monitoring the work and the assessment of the situation concerning the availability of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 00643. This is dated 8 October 1992, and here we see -- this is a conclusion: "To increase the number of members of the Council of Humanitarian Aid and Social Welfare." And here we see: "The Red Crescent commissioner shall become the tenth member of the Council of Humanitarian Aid and Social Welfare." And now, is this Council for Humanitarian Aid, is this the same coordination committee, or is this something else?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me -- Yeah. It's a poorly phrased question on my part. You know, I take full responsibility for that. Okay. Are we speaking -- when it says here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This time, Mr. Karnavas, I think the question was okay, but the answer was a bit difficult. Do you prefer red or blue? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Council for Humanitarian Aid, what is it referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's a coordinating committee for collection and reception.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we go on to the next document, and it's sort of been spliced for -- for convenience, but I think that you have the original one. This is document 1D 02662. This is a chart on humanitarian aid distribution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know who prepared this chart?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the right top corner, you can see exactly who did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The idea was done by Mrs. Antonije Jurisic, a member of the Red Cross staff, and Mr. Zeljko Coric and Goran Zunic prepared this diagram. They were also working with the Red Cross. Mr. Zeljko Coric was head of the office for IP support of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: IT support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we don't see the Red Crescent here. Is there a reason for that, on this chart, or is it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: The reason is that this chart was made before they joined this committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: There's also Merhamet missing here. This is just an idea of how to design the work of the coordinating committee. As we can see here, there are only six organisations participating at the time, and the tenth one was the Red Crescent. However, the principle was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Whether it consisted of one or more organisations, the way of keeping records, processing the data relating to the aid supplied and the mode of distribution was identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, very briefly, and if -- if the Bench has questions I'm sure they'll ask. If we look at the left -- the left bottom of this -- of this chart, we see "Local communes." Do you see that? And then there's 1, 2, 3. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Unless you tell me, I don't know, so -- now -- and then we see some lines. What is that reflecting?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: These lines represent actual distribution of aid at the local levels in local communes and other communities. The aid was distributed that was received by any of these organisations on the coordinating committee. The aid would be loaded to the truck of the representative of the local commune. He would then go back to his local commune, prepare and organise the distribution in accordance with the information that we presented earlier. This coordinating committee also agreed for certain institutions to be given priority in receiving humanitarian aid, certain humanitarian aid, and that was soup kitchens; students; dormitories where internally displaced persons and refugees were housed; also, the old people's home; the nursery; and also the hospital in terms of medical aid; and finally the civilian protection when it came to the distribution of aid that was appropriate to be received by them; and of course, all modes of organised accommodation that were either existing at the time or were later established in order to help accommodate the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, if we go on to the next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we still have this document, and you are the author of this document since your name is on it. This is something I'm interested in. "Donatori." It says "sponsor" in English. This heading is the one I'm interested in. Who were the sponsors, these donatori, these people who provided aid? Can you give us any instances of this?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that the word "sponsor" is an appropriate one as far as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English translation, it's been translated by "sponsors."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should read "donors," but this is besides the point now. Various donors, that is to say people who organised themselves abroad in order to collect aid for Bosnia-Herzegovina and Mostar, as well as other humanitarian organisations who were self-organised abroad and came to our areas bringing humanitarian aid, and if Your Honours allow me, I can show you in my report a list of some 15 or 16 organisations that made donations in 1993 -- in 2003 to Red Cross. That's page 15 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the number of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If -- if I could. Hold on one second, please. This would be from the document 1D 02651, and it's page 13, Your Honours, in that document. And of course, there's a list of the donors. If you want to put it on the ELMO, we could do that and everyone can look at it, but it's the Maltese Knights, Association of Italian Solidarity, Soros Foundation, Agape, UNHCR, Care International, ICRC, Red Cross Grude, Caritas - Cathedral, UNICEF, Red Cross Posusje, the Turney school, Bergamo, CK Lugo, Terre Des Hommes, Church World Service, IRC, Red Cross Germany, CGIL Veneto, and so on. There are 28, and then there's a list of addresses, the cities where these donors are from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, I can add something to this. Each of these organisations who were participant had a list of their donors, and the list was much longer. This is just the list of organisations that were cooperating at the time with the Red Cross, and this is the litigation that we had, an overview of the total quantity of aid that reached our area at the time, and that we agreed and coordinated together how we were going to distribute this aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02572. This is May 4th, 1993. This is to the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees, Mostar. Now, was this to the municipality of Mostar, this office?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's what I'm asking you. So it belongs to the Mostar municipality. Now, do you know Mr. Demirovic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what was he at the time? It says "President." President of what?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: He was the president of the SDA regional committee in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at the very first line, it says here: "A large quantity of seed arrived to the port of Ploce via the Fund for the Assistance to the Muslims of the Republic of BiH." And then it goes on to say: "Regional SDA Committee for Herzegovina and Merhamet Mostar are charged with distribution and storage of humanitarian aid ..." and so on. If we keep reading, we see that some aid is to remain in Mostar while other aid is to continue onwards. And my first question to you is, was this usual for this a political party, a regional political party, SDA, to be involved with humanitarian organisations such as Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I have never seen this document before, and I found it -- find it very illogical to see direct involvement of a political party in the work of a humanitarian organisation. That never happened with our organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And when it talks about seed, do you know what kind of seed they're talking about, keeping in mind what gets planted around there.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can only suppose that it was potato or wheat or something that was suitable for sowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a question in this regard, Witness. Is it acceptable or is it accepted, even, that an organisation provides humanitarian aid and says it is destined only for a part of the population of an area, like here? This is apparently a Muslim organisation, and they only want to assist Muslims. Now, is that legitimate, or should the wish be disregarded and the aid be distributed equally amongst all those who need it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my view it was something that happened on the ground. There was a fund for assistance for the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if it acted by distributing food to Muslims only, then it was not acceptable. However, if part of the aid received by Merhamet, the aid was received through the coordinating committee, then it couldn't happen that this aid would be distributed solely to the Muslims but to all the needy. I also have to tell you that the issues relating to humanitarian aid were very - how shall I put it? - or -- provided a chance for manipulations, and that is the reason why we in Mostar wanted to introduce some order in this area and to provide aid to all the people in need irrespective of who they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, two minutes before we finish. It might be better to resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, because the next question will probably last longer than two minutes, Your Honour, the answer that is, so this would be a good spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have had two hours and ten minutes, for your information. Witness, as I told you, you are now a witness of the court, and you may not contact anyone. As you know, we shall meet again tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00 since we are sitting in the afternoon tomorrow. So much for that. Mr. Stringer, I hope you might be able to give us your positions orally tomorrow in light of the requests made by the Trial Chamber. I wish all and everyone a pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just inform everyone that I will unfortunately be absent tomorrow. I'll be in again the day after tomorrow.
